title: "Parallel derivation"
description: "Measured speed-up, serial fraction and memory of the tiled, multi-worker SGB derivation, and why serial derivation is sufficient."
scgsim-kind: "research"
scgsim-status: "CONVERGING"
scgsim-id: "docs/research/geometry-build/parallelism"

**Question.** The derivation can be cut into tiles and run by several workers. What does that buy, what limits it, and is it needed?

**Result.** The best speed-up of the derivation is 1.22 times at 1,000 features, 1.26 times at 5,000 and 1.17 times at 20,000. Over the whole path from derivation to a loaded and checked model at 20,000 features, the same schedule saves 8.9 s of 209.8 s, which is a factor of 1.04. About half of the derivation time is in serial stages, so the derivation itself cannot exceed 1.98 times with this decomposition. Tiling did not lower the memory of the parent process. Every one of the nine schedules produced the same identity digest and passed validation at every size.

**Conclusion.** Serial derivation is sufficient. It takes 61.6 s at 20,000 features and scales almost linearly ([Scaling with chip size](scaling.qmd)); most of the remaining time of the path is not derivation ([Direct writer and Gmsh load](emission-and-load.qmd)); and parallelism changes neither. Parallel speed-up is not a goal of this design.

## Schedules

A **tile** is a rectangular part of the model's pixel grid; the model is cut into T × T tiles, and each tile is derived as its own job. A **worker** is a process that runs jobs. The derivation was measured under nine schedules: one tile, and 4 × 4 or 8 × 8 tiles each with 1, 8, 16 and 32 workers, on a machine with 64 hardware threads. The one-tile run is the baseline; **speed-up** is the baseline derivation time divided by the time of the schedule. Six of the 21 derivation stages run in parallel; the others always run serially.

::: {.askr-table-compact .askr-table-numeric}
{{< include figures/parallel-table.md >}}
:::

The cells give derivation and validation time and, in brackets, the speed-up.

## Speed-up

![Left: speed-up of the derivation against the number of workers for 4 × 4 tiles (solid) and 8 × 8 tiles (dashed), with the limit set by the serial stages at 20,000 features (dotted). Right: the twelve longest derivation stages at 20,000 features in one process, serial stages in orange and parallel stages in blue.](figures/parallel.svg){#fig-parallel fig-alt="Left: lines of speed-up for three sizes and two tile counts against 1, 8, 16 and 32 workers; all lie between 0.9 and 1.3 and flatten after 8 workers, far below a dotted line at about 1.98. Right: horizontal bars of stage time; noding_kernels about 9.8 seconds, assembly_faces 8.7, dissolution 7.0, shells 6.0, atomic_ids 5.6, and smaller stages below."}

In @fig-parallel the speed-up reaches its level at 8 workers and does not rise with more of them. At 20,000 features with 4 × 4 tiles the build takes 53.6 s with 8 workers, 53.2 s with 16 and 53.1 s with 32. With a single worker, tiling makes the build slower than the baseline: 0.89 to 0.92 times at 20,000 features.

## The serial fraction

Serial stages take about half of the time of all stages when the derivation runs in one process. By Amdahl's law, the speed-up of the whole derivation cannot exceed the total time divided by the serial time, even with unlimited workers.

::: {.askr-table-compact .askr-table-numeric}
{{< include figures/amdahl-table.md >}}
:::

At 20,000 features the limit is 1.98 times and the best measured speed-up 1.17 times. With workers, the serial stages become slightly longer (29.7 s in one process, 32.0 to 32.7 s with workers).

The longest stages at 20,000 features, in one process and with 4 × 4 tiles and 16 workers:

::: {.askr-table-compact .askr-table-numeric}
{{< include figures/stage-table.md >}}
:::

The four longest serial stages add up to 22.5 s, 38% of the time of all stages, and none of them became faster with workers. The parallel stages gained unevenly: `noding_kernels`, the longest, 1.61 times, `shells` 1.17 times, and `atomic_ids` 3.31 times. These measurements show which stages did not speed up; they do not show why.

## Memory {#memory}

::: {.askr-table-compact .askr-table-numeric}
{{< include figures/memory-table.md >}}
:::

The table gives the peak memory (MB) of the parent process. At 20,000 features tiling with one worker leaves it where it was (1,975 to 1,979 MB against 2,000 MB), and tiling with workers raises it by 10% to 12% (2,207 to 2,233 MB). The workers' own peaks are 2,001 to 2,030 MB at that size. A worker's peak counts memory it shares with the parent, so the values cannot be added to give the memory of the machine.

## End to end {#end-to-end}

At 20,000 features the one-process path from the derived model to a loaded and checked model takes 209.8 s: 61.6 s of derivation and 148.1 s of everything after it. The best derivation schedule (8 × 8 tiles and 8 workers, 52.7 s) brings the path to 200.8 s, a factor of 1.04. If the derivation reached the limit of the serial stages, the path would take 179 s, a factor of 1.17. The steps after the derivation (the write, the reports, the sidecar, the Gmsh load and the check on the loaded model) are not part of the derivation, so its tiles and workers do not change them; the writer has a worker setting of its own, which saves 4.7 s at this size. The steps are listed in [Direct writer and Gmsh load](emission-and-load.qmd#what-follows-the-derivation).

## Interpretation

Parallel derivation gives at most 1.26 times on the derivation and 1.04 times on the whole path. Half of the derivation is serial, and at 20,000 features the derivation is 61.6 s of the 209.8 s path. Serial derivation already scales almost linearly and takes about a minute at that size, so the design does not rely on parallel speed-up and this study does not pursue it. Adding workers beyond 8 did not shorten the build; the measurements do not show why, so they do not say whether other tile layouts or a different decomposition would do better.
